summary: In France the roof rat falls on the wrong side of a purely taxonomic line. The official domestic-animals list (Arrêté du 11 août 2006) names only captive strains of Rattus norvegicus among the Muridae — so Rattus rattus is legally 'non-domestic,' which pulls it into the Code de l'environnement's regime for espèces non domestiques. In practice a hobbyist with a small number of captive-bred roof rats must file a prefectural déclaration de détention (but not the harder certificat de capacité, which only kicks in above ~40 adult mammals), register each animal in the national I-FAP file within 8 days, and use an attestation de cession for any transfer. The good news: R. rattus is NOT on the EU invasive-species Union list (Reg. 1143/2014) or France's metropolitan invasive Arrêté, so there's no keeping/sale ban. The wrinkle: the 2021 animal-welfare law created a 'positive list' for pet species (Art. L413-1A) that, as of 2026, still hasn't been published — leaving the regime in limbo and opening a concrete advocacy window to request R. rattus's inclusion.

kit.problem: In France the pet roof rat (Rattus rattus) is treated differently from the ordinary fancy rat because of taxonomy, not because of how the animal lives. The official list of domestic animals (Arrêté du 11 août 2006) names only captive strains of the brown rat, Rattus norvegicus, among the rodents. Because the roof rat is a different species, it is classified as non-domestic, even when it is captive-bred, hand-tame, and has never lived in the wild. That taxonomic line pulls a tame pet rat into the framework for non-domestic species under the Code de l'environnement: before acquiring one, the keeper must file a prefectural déclaration de détention, register each animal in the national I-FAP file within eight days, and use an attestation de cession for any transfer. A fancy-rat keeper has none of these obligations. The already-permitted fancy rat (Rattus norvegicus) is itself the wild brown rat, domesticated only in the 19th century, so a captive-bred Rattus rattus is the same case one species over. Separately, the 2021 animal-welfare law (Loi 2021-1539, Art. L413-1A) created a forthcoming positive list of non-domestic species that may be kept as companion animals, but the implementing arrêté has not been published (confirmed by a November 2025 Sénat written question). The regime is in limbo, and captive-bred Rattus rattus could be left off the list when it is drawn up.
kit.ask: Ask the Ministre chargé de l'environnement (the minister who, under Art. L413-1A, fixes the positive list) to examine captive-bred, indoor-kept Rattus rattus for inclusion on the forthcoming positive list of non-domestic companion species, so that a tame, captive-bred roof rat is treated like the fancy rat it resembles in practice, rather than carrying declaration and registration burdens based on its Latin name. The relevant test is domestication, not wild ancestry. The dog descends from the wolf and the cat from a wild felid, yet both are recognised as domestic animals, because what defines a domestic animal is generations of captive breeding for tameness, not the species label. A captive-bred R. rattus is domesticated in that same sense. The already-permitted fancy rat (Rattus norvegicus) is itself the wild brown rat, domesticated only in the 19th century, so a captive-bred Rattus rattus is the same case one species over (see https://blonderoofrat.com/how-the-sewer-rat-became-the-fancy-rat/ ). Anyone may make this request in writing under Art. L413-1A, and the minister owes a reasoned reply within six months. When the draft arrêté goes out for public comment, also submit a short contribution on the official public-consultation portal supporting inclusion.
kit.branch_note: This is the legislature/rulemaking-window branch, not the bureaucracy-misreading branch. The agencies (préfecture, OFB) are applying the law correctly: the Arrêté du 11 août 2006 lists only Rattus norvegicus strains as domestic, so a préfet who classes Rattus rattus as non-domestic and asks for a déclaration de détention is doing what the texts require. Writing to OFB or a préfecture to complain will not change this; they cannot rewrite a national list, and they are not misapplying anything. The fix is at the rulemaking level. The 2021 welfare law (Loi 2021-1539, Art. L413-1A) created the lever: a forthcoming positive list of non-domestic species allowed as companion animals, fixed by an arrêté of the minister responsible for the environment. Art. L413-1A expressly invites "toute personne physique ou morale" to request that a species be examined for inclusion, with a reasoned ministerial answer due within six months and judicial review available. Because the implementing arrêté is still unpublished (Sénat written question qSEQ251106679, Nov. 2025, awaiting answer; April 2025 IGEDD-CGAAER report urged publication and ANSES coordination), there is a statutorily-invited window to get captive-bred Rattus rattus onto the list before it is finalized, and to avoid a de-facto ban if the species is omitted. The target is the Ministry (which holds the pen on the arrêté) via the formal L413-1A inclusion request, plus the official public-consultation portal when the draft arrêté is posted. This is not an individual-representative matter, because the underlying statute already exists; what is missing is the executive instrument (the arrêté) and the species' place on it.
kit.time_sensitive: The implementing arrêté establishing the Art. L413-1A "positive list" of non-domestic companion species is still unpublished as of late 2025 (Sénat written question qSEQ251106679, Nov. 2025, awaiting government reply; an April 2025 IGEDD-CGAAER report recommended publishing it and assigning coordination to ANSES). This means the list is being prepared now — the moment to request that captive-bred Rattus rattus be examined for inclusion is BEFORE the arrêté is finalized. No specific public-comment window for this arrêté is open at the time of writing; watch the official public-consultation portal (consultations-publiques.developpement-durable.gouv.fr, "Eau et biodiversité") for the draft to appear.

Under L413-1A any person may request that a species be examined for inclusion, with a reasoned reply due within six months. This is the official, secure electronic contact form (FranceConnect or email identification; acknowledgment within 10 business days). template.en:
Subject: Request under Article L413-1A to examine captive-bred Rattus rattus for the positive list

To the Direction de l'eau et de la biodiversité, Ministère de la Transition écologique,

I am writing about the legal status of the pet roof rat (Rattus rattus). It is classed as a non-domestic species because the domestic-animals list (Arrêté du 11 août 2006) names only Rattus norvegicus among rodents. As a result, a captive-bred, hand-tame roof rat carries declaration and I-FAP registration burdens that an identical fancy rat does not, a difference based on the animal's Latin name, with no ecological rationale for animals that are bred in captivity, kept indoors, and never released.

Under Article L413-1A of the Code de l'environnement, I request that captive-bred Rattus rattus be examined for inclusion on the forthcoming positive list of non-domestic species that may be kept as companion animals.

These animals are captive-bred, tame, kept exclusively indoors, and never released into the wild. The relevant test is domestication, not wild ancestry. The dog descends from the wolf and the cat from a wild felid, yet both are recognised as domestic animals, because what defines a domestic animal is generations of captive breeding for tameness, not its Latin name. A captive-bred roof rat is domesticated in that same sense. The already-permitted fancy rat (Rattus norvegicus) is itself the wild brown rat, domesticated only in the 19th century, so a captive-bred Rattus rattus is the same case one species over.

Thank you for your consideration. I would be grateful for your reasoned reply within the six-month period provided by Article L413-1A.

[Your name]
[Town / department]
[Date]
template.fr:
Objet: Demande au titre de l'article L413-1A d'examen du Rattus rattus né en captivité en vue de la liste positive

À l'attention de la Direction de l'eau et de la biodiversité, Ministère de la Transition écologique,

Je vous saisis au sujet du statut juridique du rat des toits de compagnie (Rattus rattus). Il est classé parmi les espèces non domestiques au motif que la liste des animaux domestiques (arrêté du 11 août 2006) ne mentionne, parmi les rongeurs, que le Rattus norvegicus. De ce fait, un rat des toits né en captivité et apprivoisé entraîne des obligations de déclaration de détention et d'enregistrement I-FAP qu'un rat domestique identique n'impose pas. Cette différence est fondée sur le nom latin de l'animal, sans justification écologique pour des animaux nés en captivité, détenus en intérieur et jamais relâchés.

En application de l'article L413-1A du code de l'environnement, je sollicite l'examen de l'inscription du Rattus rattus né en captivité sur la future liste positive des espèces non domestiques pouvant être détenues comme animaux de compagnie.

Ces animaux sont nés en captivité, apprivoisés, détenus exclusivement en intérieur et jamais relâchés dans la nature. Le critère pertinent est la domestication, et non l'ascendance sauvage. Le chien descend du loup et le chat d'un félidé sauvage, et pourtant tous deux sont reconnus comme des animaux domestiques, car ce qui définit un animal domestique, ce sont des générations d'élevage en captivité pour l'apprivoisement, et non son nom latin. Un rat des toits né en captivité est domestiqué en ce sens. Le rat domestique déjà autorisé (Rattus norvegicus) est lui-même le rat brun sauvage, domestiqué seulement au XIXe siècle, de sorte qu'un Rattus rattus né en captivité relève du même cas, une espèce plus loin.

Je vous remercie de votre attention et vous saurais gré de bien vouloir m'adresser une réponse motivée dans le délai de six mois prévu par l'article L413-1A.

[Votre nom]
[Commune / département]
[Date]

kit.confidence_notes: Verified via web: (1) Art. L413-1A of the Code de l'environnement (Légifrance) confirms the positive list is fixed by an arrêté of the minister responsible for the environment, revised every three years, and that "toute personne physique ou morale" may request a species' examination for inclusion, with a reasoned ministerial reply due within six months and administrative-court review available. (2) The implementing arrêté is still unpublished — confirmed by Sénat written question qSEQ251106679 (Sen. Jadot, Nov. 2025, still "en attente de réponse"), which also cites an April 2025 IGEDD-CGAAER report recommending publication and ANSES coordination. (3) contact.ecologie.gouv.fr is the official ministry electronic contact form (Ordinance 2014-1330; acknowledgment within 10 business days). (4) consultations-publiques.developpement-durable.gouv.fr ('Eau et biodiversité') is the official public-comment portal; checked on access — no positive-list/non-domestic-animal consultation was open (the only animal item was an unrelated Pyrenees brown-bear deterrence draft, 8-29 June 2026). Grounding facts from fr.json (Arrêté 11 août 2006 lists only R. norvegicus; R. rattus absent from the EU Union list and the metropolitan invasive Arrêté du 14 fév. 2018) are consistent with prior research but were not each re-verified line-by-line in this pass. Uncertain/u/watch items: the exact future timeline for the arrêté (government had not answered the Sénat question at last check); whether ANSES will run the technical assessment (recommended, not yet formalized); and the precise Annexe-2 threshold separating déclaration de détention from certificat de capacité for this species (flagged needs_verification in fr.json). The OFB contact directory has no national email/form and OFB does not write the list, so it was intentionally excluded as a target. This is a research aid, not legal advice; OPSEC-clean (no individual civil servant named).

keep.why: R. rattus is non-domestic (only R. norvegicus strains are on the Arrêté du 11 août 2006 domestic list), so it's governed by Code de l'environnement Art. L413-1 et seq. + the Arrêté du 8 octobre 2018 (mod. 5 sept. 2025). Below the threshold (generally ~40 adult mammals) a hobbyist needs only a prefectural déclaration de détention — not a certificat de capacité — filed before acquisition, plus I-FAP registration. Not banned (R. rattus absent from the EU Union list + metropolitan invasive Arrêté). ⚠️ The 2021 positive-list (L413-1A) is still unpublished as of 2026, so the pre-existing declaration regime continues.
keep.governing_law: Arrêté du 11 août 2006 (domestic list — R. norvegicus only); Code de l'environnement Art. L413-1 à L413-5; Arrêté du 8 octobre 2018 (mod. Arrêté du 5 sept. 2025), Annexe 2; Loi 2021-1539 Art. 14 / Art. L413-1A.

breed.why: Hobby breeding (élevage d'agrément) extends detention: below the certificat-de-capacité threshold (~40 adult mammals) only the prefectural déclaration de détention is required; above it, a certificat de capacité (Art. L413-2) and possibly an autorisation d'ouverture d'établissement (Art. L413-3) apply. No specific ban on breeding captive R. rattus. The L413-1A 'élevage de conservation' carve-out awaits its implementing decree.
breed.governing_law: Code de l'environnement Art. L413-2, L413-3; Arrêté du 8 octobre 2018, Annexe 2; Loi 2021-1539 Art. 14.

sell_give.why: Transfer of a non-domestic animal is legal but procedural: an attestation de cession (two copies) under Art. R413-1 et seq. + registration of each animal in the national I-FAP file within 8 days of acquisition. A private person may give animals away but cannot sell commercially to the public without being a declared pet-trade establishment (animalerie) under Code rural Art. L214-6. No EU sale ban (R. rattus not on the Union list).
sell_give.governing_law: Code de l'environnement Art. R413-1 et seq. (cession + I-FAP); Code rural Art. L214-6; Reg. (EU) 1143/2014 (R. rattus not listed).

transport.why: Intra-EU non-commercial movement of pet rodents has no EU passport/health-certificate scheme like cats/dogs, but the French déclaration de détention + I-FAP registration must be satisfied; an attestation de cession is needed if ownership changes. IMPORT from a non-EU country requires a veterinary health certificate per the Arrêté du 19 juillet 2002 (Annexe 18 model for rodents), limited to 5 specimens per non-commercial movement. R. rattus is not on the EU Union list, so no import ban. ⚠️ French OVERSEAS territories (Réunion, Martinique, Polynésie) actively manage R. rattus as invasive — local rules there may restrict.
transport.governing_law: Arrêté du 19 juillet 2002 (Annexe 18 — rodent import health cert); Code de l'environnement (déclaration + I-FAP); Reg. (EU) 1143/2014 Art. 7; Arrêté du 14 février 2018 (metropolitan invasive list — R. rattus absent).

restrictions.summary: Because R. rattus is 'non-domestic' in France, file a prefectural déclaration de détention BEFORE acquiring one (online or registered mail) and register each animal in the national I-FAP file within 8 days. A certificat de capacité is only required above the ~40-adult-mammal threshold. Keep the paperwork — it's the difference between a legal hobby and an offence.
steps: File a déclaration de détention with the préfecture (DDT/DREAL) before acquisition
Register each animal in I-FAP within 8 days of acquisition

forms.name: Déclaration de détention d'animaux non domestiques

restrictions.summary: Importing from outside the EU needs a veterinary health certificate (Arrêté du 19 juillet 2002, Annexe 18 model for rodents), max 5 specimens per non-commercial movement. French overseas territories manage R. rattus as invasive — check local prefectoral rules there. Never release a roof rat.

inquiry_focus: (1) Annexe 2 of the Arrêté du 8 octobre 2018 (mod. sept. 2025): is Rattus rattus listed by name (or genus Rattus / non-domestic rodents via catch-all), and what exact numerical threshold (column a/b/c) separates a déclaration de détention from a certificat de capacité for this species? (2) The positive-list arrêté under Art. L413-1A (Loi 2021-1539) is not yet published — what is the timeline, and what is the procedure to formally request that captive-bred Rattus rattus be evaluated for inclusion as a companion species? (3) For intra-EU transport of a captive-bred R. rattus by a private individual with no change of ownership, is any documentation/notification required beyond the détention paperwork, and does TRACES apply?
